The search located the paper but did not return its equation, so I can't confirm the formula from these results.

The paper is Riley, Linker, and Arge, "On the Role Played by Magnetic Expansion Factor in the Prediction of Solar Wind Speed," a 2015 manuscript (the preprint is dated January 2015) hosted on Pete Riley's Predictive Science site. Its central argument is that the expansion factor's role in the WSA model has become small, with distance from the coronal hole boundary (DCHB) doing most of the work. The authors show that the WSA model has evolved so much that the role played by the expansion factor term is now largely minimal, being supplanted by the distance from the coronal hole boundary. They also found that the DCHB- and WSA-driven models tend to produce better estimates of solar parameters at 1 AU than the WS model, particularly when pseudo-streamers are present.

Secondary sources describe the same conclusion. One reports that Riley and colleagues concluded expansion factor plays "only an indirect role" in determining the speed at 1 AU. A Springer review notes that the calculation of f is more sensitive to noise, data gaps, and zero-point problem than DCHB, which may partially explain the poorer correlation of the WS model.

For the equation itself, you'd need to open the full PDF at predsci.com or the published version in Space Weather, since none of these results show the formula.

The paper is arXiv:2003.09336, submitted March 20, 2020. It is published in The Astrophysical Journal, vol. 891, no. 2, article 165, DOI 10.3847/1538-4357/ab78a0.

- **Scope:** The paper presents an adaptive system that uses in situ solar wind measurements to adjust WSA model solutions near the Sun so they better match conditions near Earth. It fuses information from in situ measurements of the solar wind into numerical models. It also introduces a new Tunable HUX (THUX) model and runs a statistical analysis for 2006–2015 (the newly developed Tunable HUX (THUX) model which solves the viscous form of the underlying Burgers equation. We perform a statistical analysis of the resulting solar wind predictions for the time 2006-2015.).
- **Coefficients:** The search results describe the structure of the method. Section 4.1 is a sensitivity analysis that ranks WSA coefficients by their impact on output and removes the least influential ones. Section 4.2 covers building an ensemble, and Section 4.3 selects the optimum coefficients and derives confidence boundaries (They identify the model coefficients that have the lowest impact on the model output and deduce the ranking of the coefficients. By removing these coefficients from the adaptive prediction scheme, we reduce the computational complexity and processor requirements as much as possible.). I did not get the actual coefficient values or the ranking results from these snippets.
- **Predecessor:** Paper I (arXiv:1905.04353) covers the operational framework, using PFSS and Schatten current sheet magnetic field models with the WSA relation on Carrington Rotation 2077.
- **Accepted manuscript:** A Goddard-hosted accepted version is available at reading-clone.eprints-hosting.org/90943. The ar5iv HTML rendering of arXiv:2003.09336 is also indexed.

To get the specific coefficient values and the ranking table, the arXiv PDF or ar5iv page for 2003.09336 would need to be read directly.

**WSA equation (Eq. 12):**

$$v_{\text{wsa}}(f_{\text{p}},d)=v_0+\frac{(v_1-v_0)}{(1+f_{\text{p}})^{\alpha}}\left\{\beta-\gamma\exp\left[-(d/w)^{\delta}\right]\right\}^{3}$$

**Coefficients:** The page gives them in one line, not a table: "For the coefficients in Eq.(12) we use v0=285, v1=910, α=2/9, β=1, γ=0.8, w=2, and δ=3." Your value of 625 does not appear in the text.

**Citations for the form:** The page attributes the WSA model to Arge et al. 2003, "Improved Method for Specifying Solar Wind Speed Near the Sun," in *AIP Conference Series*, vol. 679, pp. 190–193. It does not cite McGregor 2011 or Riley 2015 for the WSA form. Riley et al. 2015 appears only for the role of expansion factor and the three empirical relationships in general. McGregor et al. 2008 is cited for the PFSS–SCS coupling, not the WSA form. Arge 2004 is not cited.

**Radius:** The page says the empirical relationships specify speed "at a reference sphere of 5R0 (or 30R0 for the MAS model)." So the WSA speed is evaluated at 5 R0, the outer boundary of the coronal model, and the HUX model then maps it to 1 au (215 R0). It is not computed at the 2.5 R0 source surface.

**Optimized coefficients:** None are reported. The authors say optimization is deferred to a subsequent paper.

**Journal volume and article number:** The page gives only the conference volume (679) and page range (190–193) for Arge et al. 2003. It gives no article number.

**WSA velocity equation (Eq. 4):**

$$v_{\text{wsa}}(f_p,d)=c_1+\frac{c_2}{(1+f_p)^{c_3}}\left\{c_4-c_5\exp\left[-\left(\frac{d}{c_6}\right)^{c_7}\right]\right\}^{c_8}$$

**Coefficients, defaults, and ensemble ranges**

| Coefficient | Default | Ensemble range |
|---|---|---|
| c1 | 250 km/s | ±4% in 2% steps (example) |
| c2 | 650 km/s | ±4% in 2% steps (example) |
| c3 | 0.29 | ±4% in 2% steps (example) |
| c4 | 1 | ±4% in 2% steps (example) |
| c5 | 0.8 | Not varied |
| c6 | 3° | Not varied |
| c7 | 1.75 | Not varied |
| c8 | 3 | Not varied |

The example uses the set L = [−4, −2, 0, 2, 4] percent for c1–c4, giving 5⁴ = 625 members. Seven η values for the THUX model multiply this to 4,375 solutions at Earth. The η list appears to contain a typo: −10e−9 is listed twice and no +10e−9 value appears.

**Sensitivity ranking**

- The WSA output is most sensitive to c4, then c1, c3, and c2, in that order.
- The other coefficients have considerably smaller influence. The paper does not rank c5–c8 explicitly, but they were screened out of the ensemble.

**Optimum coefficients over time**

- The paper does not report specific optimum coefficient values.
- At each step, the top 1,000 solutions from the previous Carrington Rotation update the coefficients for the next one, and the ensemble median is used as the prediction.
- Coefficient variation is capped at 4 percent to limit overfitting.
- Extending the training window to 5 rotations gave no significant improvement.

**Reported skill (CR2047–2167, at Earth)**

| Model | RMSE (km/s) | MAE (km/s) | PCC |
|---|---|---|---|
| WSA (default) | 111.0 | 91.1 | 0.43 |
| Adaptive-WSA (ED) | 93.6 | 75.4 | 0.50 |
| WS (default) | 99.4 | 77.0 | 0.29 |
| Adaptive-WS (ED) | 90.1 | 69.4 | 0.41 |
| DCHB (default) | 103.3 | 81.1 | 0.34 |
| Adaptive-DCHB (ED) | 92.7 | 71.9 | 0.45 |

- The paper reports RMSE improvements of roughly 10–15 percent for the adaptive models.
- THUX alone, without the adaptive step, reduced WSA RMSE to 107.8 km/s and raised the correlation coefficient to 0.45.
- The 27-day persistence baseline has an RMSE of 121.6 km/s.

**STEREO**

The body text does not mention STEREO in situ data. The only in situ data cited is ACE/SWEPAM at Earth/L1. The reference list was truncated in the content provided, so I can't fully rule out a STEREO-related citation there.

The search turned up the 2015 Riley, Linker & Arge paper in *Space Weather* (vol. 13, pp. 154–169), but none of the results contain the specific parameter values in your query (285, 625, 2/9, w = 2), so I can't confirm those.

- **Main finding:** The paper argues that the expansion factor's role in WSA has shrunk, with the distance-from-coronal-hole-boundary term doing most of the work. The authors show that the WSA model has evolved so far that the expansion factor term is now largely minimal, supplanted by the DCHB.
- **Model comparison:** The authors compare the Wang-Sheeley (WS), DCHB, and WSA models against in situ data. DCHB- and WSA-driven models generally estimate 1 AU solar parameters better than the WS model, especially when pseudostreamers are present. A related source notes that WSA and DCHB produce similar results because the slow wind in WSA comes mainly from the DCHB term.
- **Model structure:** WSA approaches the WS model as γ goes to zero, and approaches DCHB as α goes to zero. The paper's hypercube table lists parameter search ranges for each model, including α, w, and δ for WSA (for example, α from 0.3 to 0.5 and w from 0.1 to 0.4). Those ranges are the closest match to your parameter query, but they are not the values you cited.
- **Physical interpretation:** The authors suggest their results provide tentative support for boundary layer theories of the slow solar wind's origin.

For the exact values you're asking about, the full paper is at doi 10.1002/2014SW001144, and the Wiley full-text link is in the results.
